'''Proportionate reduction of error (PRE)''' is the gain in precision of predicting dependent variable <math>y</math> from knowing the independent variable <math>x</math> (or a collection of multiple variables). It is a [[goodness of fit]] measure of statistical models, and forms the mathematical basis for several correlation coefficients.<ref>Freeman, L.C.: Elementary applied statistics, New, York, London, Sidney (John Wiley and Sons) 1965</ref> The summary statistics is particularly useful and popular when used to evaluate models where the dependent variable is binary, taking on values {0,1}.

== Example ==
If both <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> vectors have cardinal (interval or rational) scale, then without knowing <math>x</math>, the best predictor for an unknown <math>y</math> would be <math>\bar{y}</math>, the arithmetic mean of the <math>y</math>-data. The total prediction error would be <math>E_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n{(y_i - \bar{y})^2}</math> .

If, however, <math>x</math> and a function relating <math>y</math> to <math>x</math> are known, for example a straight line <math>\hat{y}_i = a + b x_i</math>, then the prediction error becomes <math>E_2 = \sum_{i=1}^n{(y_i - \hat{y})^2}</math>. The [[coefficient of determination]] then becomes <math>r^2 = \frac{E_1 - E_2}{E_1} = 1 - \frac{E_2}{E_1}</math> and is the fraction of variance of <math>y</math> that is explained by <math>x</math>. Its [[square root]] is Pearson's [[product-moment correlation]] <math>r</math>.

There are several other correlation coefficients that have PRE interpretation and are used for variables of different scales:
